puntos: Own resources: new outlets, new products
Join with or buy other businesses

visual.veredicto: Speed versus control: it depends on finance, risk and the market

turnos.t: How do firms grow? Two routes.
Internal growth, also called organic growth, is growth achieved using a business's own resources, such as opening new outlets or developing new products.
External growth, or inorganic growth, is growth achieved by joining with or buying other businesses.
Take the app's invented case: FitNow, forty gyms in Spain with eighteen million euros of revenue, wants to enter Portugal.
Opening its own gyms one by one is internal growth: slower, but lower risk, with full control of its culture.
Buying PortoFit, twenty-five gyms, for thirty million euros is external growth: sixty-five gyms overnight, local knowledge, one rival fewer.
But it costs more than a year's revenue, and cultures may clash.

escenas.titulo: Why grow, and why stay small?

puntos: Economies of scale: lower average cost
Spread risk across products and markets
A manageable life for the owner

visual.veredicto: Depends on the market and the owner's objectives

turnos.t: Why grow?
For economies of scale, so lower average cost.
For market share and market power.
To spread risk across products and markets.
To survive against bigger rivals.
And because owners and managers are ambitious.
But you must also evaluate staying small.
A small firm keeps control and decides quickly.
It can give personal service to a niche that big firms ignore, like a bicycle repair shop that knows every customer.
It adapts fast, avoids diseconomies and the risk of expansion, and the owner may prefer a manageable life.
The price: higher average costs and exposure to one shock, like a big rival opening next door.
Judgement: stay small where customers pay for service; grow where price is everything.

filas: Two firms agree to join as one
Brand used for fees and royalties

turnos.t: Now the external growth methods.
A merger is when two firms agree to join and form one business.
An acquisition is when one firm buys a controlling stake in another, meaning more than fifty per cent of the shares.
Both give instant scale, but integration is hard: when two banks merge, cultures clash.
A takeover, in textbooks, usually means a hostile acquisition: buying control against the wishes of the target's managers, often by buying shares on the stock exchange.
Everyday English also uses takeover for friendly deals, so define it in your answer.
And the direction: horizontal, two gym chains; vertical backward, a bakery buying a flour mill; vertical forward, a brewery buying bars; conglomerate, unrelated businesses.

visual.pie: Shanghai Disneyland, opened 16 June 2016: a joint venture, Shendi Group 57 %, Disney 43 %

turnos.t: A joint venture is an arrangement in which two or more businesses create a new, jointly owned company to carry out a specific project, sharing costs, risks and profits.
Look at this castle.
Shanghai Disneyland opened on the sixteenth of June, twenty sixteen.
The state-owned Shanghai Shendi Group owns fifty-seven per cent of the resort, and Disney forty-three.
But Disney owns seventy per cent of the management company that runs it, so it controls the visitor experience.
Shendi brings local knowledge, government contacts and investment.
The risk: partners may disagree.
A strategic alliance is an agreement to cooperate and share resources for mutual benefit while remaining independent.
No new company: Iberia and the oneworld airlines sell each other's flights without merging.

escenas.titulo: Franchising: both sides of the deal

puntos: − One bad franchisee hurts the brand
− Initial fee and royalties on sales

visual.veredicto: 6 % royalty on €250,000 of sales = €15,000 for the franchisor

turnos.t: Franchising is an arrangement in which a franchisor allows a franchisee to use its brand and business model in exchange for an initial fee and royalties.
The franchisee opens and runs the outlet; the franchisor gives training, supplies and marketing.
A six per cent royalty on sales of two hundred and fifty thousand euros gives the franchisor fifteen thousand euros.
For the franchisor: fast growth using franchisees' capital, plus royalty income.
But less control, and one poor franchisee can damage the whole brand, so the rules are strict.
For the franchisee: a known brand and a proven model, so less risk than starting alone.
But fees, royalties, and no freedom to change the menu or logo.
Say whose side you mean.

visual.pie: Impact of MNCs on host countries, global business operations, local economic effects

turnos.t: Last box: multinational companies, and their impact on host countries.
A multinational company is a business with its headquarters in one country, the home country, that operates in at least one other country, the host country.
Disney's home is the United States; France and China are hosts.
Exporting alone is not enough: it must operate abroad.
Building or buying assets abroad is foreign direct investment: long-term investment by a business from one country in productive assets, such as factories or offices, in another country.
The multinational hires local workers, buys from local suppliers and pays taxes.
Then part of the profit is sent home.
That is repatriation of profits.

escenas.titulo: Why go abroad, and how to enter

visual.titulo: Disney abroad: two ways into host countries
filas: Minority stake; Disney managed the park

turnos.t: Why go multinational?
New markets, when home sales stop growing.
Lower costs: cheaper labour, land or materials.
Avoiding trade barriers, because producing inside a market avoids import tariffs.
Economies of scale.
And spreading risk: a slump in one country is offset elsewhere.
Then, how to enter.
Disneyland Paris opened on the twelfth of April, nineteen ninety-two, as Euro Disney: Disney took a minority stake in a listed company and managed the park.
It lost heavily at first, partly over culture.
It banned alcohol, French visitors expected wine with meals, and critics called it American cultural imperialism.
Disney lifted the ban within about a year.
In Shanghai, it chose a joint venture with a local partner.
Lesson: adapt to the host culture.

escenas.titulo: Impact on host countries: both sides

visual.titulo: Impact of MNCs on host countries
visual.veredicto: It depends: enforced laws, MNC behaviour, local reinvestment

turnos.t: Now the impact on host countries.
Positives: multinationals create direct jobs, and indirect jobs at local suppliers, often with wages above the local average.
Their investment builds productive capacity.
Local workers learn new techniques and safety standards, and those skills stay even if the firm leaves.
Governments collect taxes, and consumers get more choice.
Negatives: much of the profit is repatriated.
Local firms can be crowded out, because they can't match the multinational's prices.
Some supply chains have unsafe conditions.
Where laws are weak, firms may pollute.
And because they are footloose, able to move, they can pressure governments for tax breaks.
The top-band conclusion: it depends on enforced laws, the firm's behaviour and reinvestment.

puntos.texto: Karachi factory fire kills more than 250 garment workers
Tazreen factory fire in Dhaka kills 112 workers
Disney tells licensees to phase out Bangladesh, Pakistan, Belarus, Ecuador, Venezuela

turnos.t: Here is a pull-out decision to evaluate.
In September twenty twelve, a factory fire in Karachi, Pakistan, killed more than two hundred and fifty garment workers.
In November, the Tazreen factory fire in Dhaka, Bangladesh, killed one hundred and twelve.
On the fourth of March, twenty thirteen, Disney told its licensees to phase out Disney-branded production in Bangladesh, Pakistan, Belarus, Ecuador and Venezuela by March twenty fourteen.
Strength: it protected Disney's family-friendly brand.
Limitation: less than one per cent of Disney's factories were in Bangladesh, so the cost to Disney was small, but workers could lose jobs instead of getting safer buildings.
Critics said staying and paying for improvements would help more.
Disney said it might return if factories improved.

escenas.titulo: The UAE: a host country sets the rules

puntos.texto: Most onshore firms need a UAE national owning at least 51 %
Corporate tax: 9 % on profit above AED 375,000
Emiratisation: firms with 50+ staff reach 10 % Emiratis in skilled jobs

turnos.t: The United Arab Emirates show a host country that sets the rules.
They sit between Europe, Asia and Africa, with big ports like Jebel Ali and business-friendly free zones.
Before June twenty twenty-one, most onshore companies needed an Emirati owner with at least fifty-one per cent.
Since the first of June, twenty twenty-one, foreigners can own one hundred per cent in most activities: an incentive for investment.
From June twenty twenty-three, profits above three hundred and seventy-five thousand dirhams are taxed at nine per cent.
And Emiratisation: firms with fifty or more staff must raise the share of Emiratis in skilled jobs by two per cent a year, to ten per cent by the end of twenty twenty-six.
Incentives plus conditions.

escenas.titulo: For the exam: stakeholders, growth, MNCs

filas: Explain a conflict between two groups
Explain an economy and a diseconomy
Name type + why average cost moves
Explain two reasons to locate in UAE

turnos.t: For the exam, these are the typical questions.
Distinguish between internal and external stakeholders, two marks: a definition and an example for each.
Explain a conflict, four marks: each group's interest, the mechanism, and why they clash.
Explain one economy and one diseconomy of scale: name the type, then why average cost falls or rises.
Distinguish a joint venture from a strategic alliance: is a new company created?
Explain two reasons why multinationals locate in the Emirates: a precise fact, then why it attracts them.
And the ten-markers: examine VoltNord's conflicts, to what extent external growth suits FitNow, discuss multinationals' impact, or evaluate Disney's exit.
Define, argue both sides with case facts, then judge, with conditions.
